newsitem.title: USA: Clinton asks Americans support NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Clinton asks Americans support NATO expansion.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday urged the American people to support NATO plans to extend its security umbrella over former Soviet allies in Central Europe despite its cost and the risks to the U.S. military.
Speaking at commencement ceremonies for cadets graduating from the U.S. Military Academy, Clinton said the gains in strengthening NATO and uniting Europe outweighed the burdens involved.
"The bottom line to me is clear: Expanding NATO will enhance our security. It is the right thing to do. We must not fail history's challenge at this moment," Clinton said.

He began his push to sell Americans on the idea two days after returning from a tour of Europe during which he joined in the signing of an agreement between NATO and Russia aimed at defusing Moscow's concerns about enlarging the Western treaty alliance.
Clinton and the 15 other NATO leaders meet in July in Madrid for talks that are expected to lead to invitations for other nations to join the alliance.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic lead the field of 11 countries wanting to become the first new members of the West's military alliance since Spain in 1982.
Some members of Congress object to expansion, saying the move will increase costs for the United States and expose it to further military obligations in Europe.
On a sunny day in Michie Stadium on the tree-shaded grounds of the academy, Clinton admitted to the cadets that the benefits to expansion "are not cost- or risk-free."
He said NATO expansion is estimated to cost the United States $200 million a year for 10 years.
More important, he said, enlargement requires extending NATO's "most solemn security pledge -- to treat an attack against one as an attack against all."

"We have always made the pledge credible through the deployment of our troops and the deterrence of our nuclear weapons. In the years ahead you could be asked to put your lives on the line for a new NATO member, just as today you can be called upon to defend the freedom of our allies in Western Europe," he said.
He said the benefits of enlargement were strengthening NATO for the future, locking in democracy's gains in Central Europe, building stability across the Atlantic and uniting Europe, not dividing it.
"These gains decisively outweigh the burdens," he said.

After he spoke, Clinton, still using a cane from March 14 knee surgery, hobbled a few feet in front of the podium without his cane and presented the diplomas to each of the academy's 50 honour graduates.

Clinton on Tuesday was in Paris for the signing of an agreement between NATO and Russia setting up a joint council to try to develop a consensus on policy issues and defuse Moscow's concerns about NATO expansion.

Russia, however, will have no say in expansion of the alliance. NATO has said any former communist country wishing to be considered must have established democratic control of its armed forces, set up a market economy, and be attempting to make its forces compatible with those of the alliance.
Other who have applied for admission include Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.

U.S. officials say the earliest possible time negotiations could conclude with the first round of prospective new NATO members is late in the fall. Then if all goes according to plan NATO foreign ministers would meet in December to approve the plans and submit them to member countries for approval.

In the United States, it will take a two-thirds majority vote of the Senate's 100 members to approve amendments to the NATO treaty to include new members. The White House expects a vigorous debate. The aim is to have a ceremony bringing in the new members on the 50th anniversary of NATO's founding, in April 1999 in Washington.
